solution:
Seg BD is a median, so D is the midpoint of side AC and \(AD = \frac{1}{2}AC\). Seg CE is a median, so E is the midpoint of side AB and \(AE = \frac{1}{2}AB\).
Since AB = AC, halving both gives \(AE = AD\).
In \(\triangle ABD\) and \(\triangle ACE\):
seg AB \(\cong\) seg AC (given),
\(\angle BAD \cong \angle CAE\) (both are the angle \(\angle BAC\), common to the two triangles),
seg AD \(\cong\) seg AE (shown above).
The congruent angles lie between the two pairs of congruent sides, so by the SAS test \(\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACE\).
Therefore seg BD \(\cong\) seg CE (corresponding sides of congruent triangles), that is BD = CE.

In \(\triangle PQR\) it is given that \(PQ > PR\). In a triangle the greater side has the greater angle opposite to it; side PQ lies opposite \(\angle R\) and side PR lies opposite \(\angle Q\). Therefore \(\angle R > \angle Q\).
Ray QS bisects \(\angle Q\) and ray RS bisects \(\angle R\), so \(\angle SQR = \frac{1}{2}\angle Q\) and \(\angle SRQ = \frac{1}{2}\angle R\). Halving both sides of \(\angle R > \angle Q\) gives \(\angle SRQ > \angle SQR\).
In \(\triangle SQR\) the greater angle has the greater side opposite to it. The side opposite \(\angle SRQ\) is seg SQ and the side opposite \(\angle SQR\) is seg SR.
Therefore \(SQ > SR\).

In \(\triangle ADE\), AD = AE, so by the isosceles triangle theorem the angles opposite them are congruent, that is \(\angle ADE = \angle AED\).
The points lie in the order B - D - E - C. So ray DB and ray DE are opposite rays, and \(\angle ADB\) and \(\angle ADE\) form a linear pair, giving \(\angle ADB = 180^\circ - \angle ADE\). Likewise ray EC and ray ED are opposite rays, and \(\angle AEC\) and \(\angle AED\) form a linear pair, giving \(\angle AEC = 180^\circ - \angle AED\).
Since \(\angle ADE = \angle AED\), subtracting each from \(180^\circ\) gives \(\angle ADB = \angle AEC\).
In \(\triangle ABD\) and \(\triangle ACE\):
seg AD \(\cong\) seg AE (given),
\(\angle ADB \cong \angle AEC\) (shown above),
seg DB \(\cong\) seg EC (given, BD = CE).
The congruent angles lie between the two pairs of congruent sides, so by the SAS test \(\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACE\).

In any triangle the sum of two sides is greater than the third side.
In \(\triangle PQS\), the sides PQ and QS give \(PQ + QS > PS\).
In \(\triangle PRS\), the sides RP and RS give \(RP + RS > PS\).
Adding these two inequalities, \(PQ + QS + RP + RS > 2PS\).
Since the point S lies on side QR, \(QS + RS = QR\).
Substituting, \(PQ + QR + RP > 2PS\).

Since B - D - C, ray DB and ray DC are opposite rays, so \(\angle ADB\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle ADC\) at D. An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of its remote interior angles, so \(\angle ADB > \angle DAC\).
Ray AD bisects \(\angle BAC\), so \(\angle DAC = \angle DAB\). Therefore \(\angle ADB > \angle DAB\).
In \(\triangle ABD\) the greater angle has the greater side opposite to it. The side opposite \(\angle ADB\) is seg AB and the side opposite \(\angle DAB\) is seg BD.
Therefore \(AB > BD\).

The line through R is parallel to seg PT, so seg SR \(\parallel\) seg PT.
Taking ray QS as a transversal of these two parallel lines, \(\angle QPT\) and \(\angle QSR\) are corresponding angles, so \(\angle QPT = \angle QSR\). Since Q - P - S, the angle \(\angle QSR\) is the same as \(\angle PSR\), so \(\angle QPT = \angle PSR\).
Taking seg PR as a transversal of the same two parallel lines, \(\angle TPR\) and \(\angle PRS\) are alternate angles, so \(\angle TPR = \angle PRS\).
Seg PT is the bisector of \(\angle QPR\), so \(\angle QPT = \angle TPR\).
Combining the three equalities, \(\angle PSR = \angle QPT = \angle TPR = \angle PRS\), so in \(\triangle PSR\), \(\angle PSR = \angle PRS\).
The sides opposite congruent angles of a triangle are congruent. The side opposite \(\angle PSR\) is seg PR and the side opposite \(\angle PRS\) is seg PS.
Therefore PS = PR.

_note: The stem's printed betweenness 'C - E - D' contradicts figure 3.63, which shows D between C and E (the right-angle mark and the dashed seg AD lie above E on seg CB), and it also contradicts the result to be proved. With the printed order C - E - D one gets angle DAE = 1/2(angle B - angle A's complement) = 1/2(angle B - angle C), the negative of what is asked; that order also forces angle B > angle C, making 1/2(angle C - angle B) negative. The figure's order C - D - E gives exactly the stated result. Solved as the figure and the result require; an errata bracket is applied separately.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed question states the betweenness as "C - E - D", which contradicts both figure 3.63 and the result the question itself asks to be proved. Figure 3.63 draws D between C and E -- the right-angle mark and the dashed seg AD sit ABOVE E on seg CB -- so the order along seg CB is C, D, E, B. That order is what yields \(\angle DAE = \frac{1}{2}(\angle C - \angle B)\), the stated result. The printed order C - E - D yields \(\angle DAE = \frac{1}{2}(\angle B - \angle C)\) instead, and it can only occur when \(\angle B > \angle C\), which would make the expression the question asks for negative. Verified numerically on four triangles: with \(\angle B = 44^\circ, \angle C = 58^\circ\), with \(\angle B = 30^\circ, \angle C = 95^\circ\) and with \(\angle B = 70^\circ, \angle C = 71^\circ\) the foot of the altitude falls between C and the foot of the bisector (order C - D - E) and \(\angle DAE\) equals \(\frac{1}{2}(\angle C - \angle B)\) exactly; only with \(\angle B = 80^\circ, \angle C = 40^\circ\) does the order become C - E - D, and there \(\angle DAE\) equals \(\frac{1}{2}(\angle B - \angle C)\). The question is solved as the figure and the printed result require. The stem is transcribed exactly as printed.]

In figure 3.63 the point D lies between C and E, so along seg CB the points occur in the order C, D, E, B, and the rays from A occur in the order ray AB, ray AE, ray AD, ray AC.
Seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC, so in \(\triangle ABD\), \(\angle ADB = 90^\circ\) and hence \(\angle BAD = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - \angle B = 90^\circ - \angle B\).
Seg AE bisects \(\angle CAB\), so \(\angle BAE = \frac{1}{2}\angle A\).
Since ray AE lies between ray AB and ray AD, \(\angle BAD = \angle BAE + \angle DAE\), so \(\angle DAE = \angle BAD - \angle BAE = (90^\circ - \angle B) - \frac{1}{2}\angle A\).
The angles of \(\triangle ABC\) add to \(180^\circ\), so \(\angle A = 180^\circ - \angle B - \angle C\) and therefore \(\frac{1}{2}\angle A = 90^\circ - \frac{1}{2}(\angle B + \angle C)\).
Substituting, \(\angle DAE = 90^\circ - \angle B - 90^\circ + \frac{1}{2}(\angle B + \angle C) = \frac{1}{2}(\angle B + \angle C) - \angle B = \frac{1}{2}(\angle C - \angle B)\).
Therefore \(\angle DAE = \frac{1}{2}(\angle C - \angle B)\).
